stem: You have a dataset of emails each already labeled spam or not spam, and you want to train a model to predict that label for new emails. Which type of machine learning is this?
explanationCorrect: The training data carries known labels (spam or not spam) and the goal is to predict that label on new inputs, which is the defining setup of supervised learning.
explanationIncorrect: Unsupervised learning works on data without labels and tries to find structure on its own, such as grouping similar items, so it does not fit a problem where every example already has the answer. Reinforcement learning trains an agent by rewarding or penalizing actions it takes in an environment over time; there is no environment or reward signal here, just labeled examples. Clustering is a specific unsupervised technique for grouping unlabeled data, so it is the wrong paradigm for label prediction. Learning a mapping from labeled examples to a target label is supervised learning.

stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI?

options.text: They are nested: AI is the broadest field, machine learning is a subset of AI, deep learning is a subset of machine learning, and generative AI is built on deep learning
They are four unrelated fields with no overlap
Generative AI is the broadest field and contains artificial intelligence
Machine learning and artificial intelligence are two names for exactly the same thing

explanationCorrect: The terms nest from broad to narrow: AI is the umbrella, machine learning is one way to achieve AI, deep learning is a subset of ML using neural networks, and generative AI is a deep-learning application that creates new content.
explanationIncorrect: They are clearly related, not unrelated fields. Generative AI is a narrow, recent branch, not the broadest category that contains AI. Machine learning is one approach within AI, not a synonym for all of AI, since AI also includes techniques that are not learned from data. The correct picture is the nested hierarchy from AI down to generative AI.

stem: You want to predict a house's sale price, a continuous numeric value, from its features. Which kind of supervised learning task is this?
explanationCorrect: Predicting a continuous number such as a price is a regression task, where the model outputs a value along a range rather than a discrete label.
explanationIncorrect: Classification predicts a discrete category (such as spam or not spam), not a continuous number. Clustering is unsupervised and groups unlabeled data; it does not predict a target value. Reinforcement learning trains an agent through rewards in an environment and does not fit a labeled price-prediction problem. Predicting a continuous value is regression.

stem: You have unlabeled customer data and want to discover natural groupings of similar customers without predefined categories. Which approach fits?
explanationCorrect: With no labels and the goal of finding structure, clustering (an unsupervised technique) groups similar records together so natural segments emerge from the data itself.
explanationIncorrect: Supervised classification and regression both require labeled examples to learn a target, which you do not have here. Reinforcement learning optimizes an agent's actions against a reward signal, not grouping of static unlabeled records. Discovering groups in unlabeled data is unsupervised clustering.

stem: A model has already been trained and is now returning predictions for new incoming data in production. What is this phase called?
explanationCorrect: Using a trained model to produce predictions on new data is inference; it is the serving phase that follows training.
explanationIncorrect: Training is the earlier phase where the model learns its parameters from data, which has already happened here. Feature engineering is the preparation of input variables before training. Data labeling is annotating examples with target values for supervised training. Producing predictions from a finished model is inference.

stem: A model scores very high on its training data but performs poorly on new, unseen data. What does this most likely indicate?
explanationCorrect: Overfitting is exactly this pattern: the model has memorized the training data, including its noise, so it generalizes poorly to data it has not seen.
explanationIncorrect: Underfitting is the opposite, where the model is too simple and does poorly even on the training data. Inference hardware affects speed and cost, not the gap between training and test accuracy. Output size is unrelated to generalization. Strong training performance with weak generalization is overfitting.

stem: Which AWS service is the managed platform for building, training, and deploying your own custom machine learning models at scale?
explanationCorrect: Amazon SageMaker is the end-to-end managed ML platform for building, training, tuning, and deploying custom models, covering the full model lifecycle.
explanationIncorrect: Amazon Bedrock provides access to pre-built foundation models for generative AI; it is not where you build and train your own custom models from data. Amazon Polly is a text-to-speech service. Amazon Textract extracts text and data from documents. The custom-model build-and-train platform is Amazon SageMaker.

stem: Which AWS service gives you access to foundation models from providers such as Anthropic, Meta, and Amazon through a single API, without provisioning or managing any model infrastructure?
explanationCorrect: Amazon Bedrock is the fully managed service that exposes foundation models from multiple providers behind one API, so you can call them for text or image generation without standing up any infrastructure.
explanationIncorrect: Amazon Rekognition is a purpose-built computer vision service for detecting objects, faces, and text in images and video; it is not a gateway to general foundation models. Amazon Comprehend is a managed natural language service for tasks like sentiment analysis and entity extraction, not a catalog of generative foundation models. AWS Glue is a serverless data integration and ETL service and has nothing to do with model inference. The single-API, multi-provider foundation model service is Amazon Bedrock.

stem: You want a generative AI assistant to answer questions using your company's internal documents, keeping answers grounded in that private data, without retraining or fine-tuning the underlying model. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), retrieving relevant documents and supplying them as context to the model
Continuously pre-training the model on the public internet
Raising the model's temperature so it invents more answers

explanationCorrect: RAG retrieves the most relevant passages from your document store at query time and passes them to the model as context, so answers are grounded in your private data with no model retraining.
explanationIncorrect: Pre-training the model further on the public internet neither incorporates your private documents nor is something a practitioner does casually; it is expensive and does not target your data. Raising the temperature makes outputs more random and actually increases the chance of ungrounded, made-up answers, which is the opposite of what you want. Reducing the context window gives the model less room to read supplied material, hurting grounded answering. The technique that grounds a model in private data without retraining is Retrieval Augmented Generation.

stem: You are deploying a generative AI chat feature and must block certain harmful topics and filter unsafe content in both prompts and responses. Which Amazon Bedrock capability is purpose-built for this?
explanationCorrect: Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock let you define denied topics and content filters that are applied to both user prompts and model responses, which is exactly the responsible-use control described.
explanationIncorrect: Provisioned Throughput reserves model capacity for predictable, high-volume inference; it is a performance and cost feature, not a safety filter. Bedrock Agents orchestrate multi-step tasks by calling tools and APIs on the model's behalf; they coordinate actions rather than screen content for harm. Fine-tuning adapts a model to your data and style, but it is not a reliable topic or safety filter and does not give you configurable denied topics. The capability for content filtering and blocked topics is Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock.

domain: Security, Compliance, and Governance for AI Solutions
stem: Your security team asks whether prompts and completions sent to a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock are used to train the base models or exposed outside your account. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Bedrock does not use your prompts or completions to train the base foundation models, and your data is encrypted in transit and at rest within your account boundary
Bedrock adds all prompts to a shared public dataset that anyone can query
Bedrock requires you to email prompts to each model provider for processing
Bedrock stores your prompts unencrypted by default and shares them with other customers

explanationCorrect: Amazon Bedrock does not use your inputs or outputs to train its base foundation models, and it encrypts your data in transit and at rest, keeping it within your account, which is what a security review needs to confirm.
explanationIncorrect: Bedrock does not publish your prompts to any shared or public dataset; that would directly contradict its data-isolation model. It also does not require emailing data to providers; inference happens through the managed service API within AWS. And it does not store your data unencrypted or share it with other customers; encryption at rest and in transit is applied and data stays isolated to your account. The accurate statement is that Bedrock keeps your data private, encrypted, and out of base-model training.

stem: What is a foundation model?

options.text: A large model pre-trained on broad, unlabeled data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks
A small model trained to perform exactly one narrow task
A rules engine built entirely from hand-written if-then logic
A database that stores cached answers to look up

explanationCorrect: A foundation model is trained once on a broad corpus and can then be applied or adapted to many tasks (summarization, Q&A, generation), which is what makes it foundational.
explanationIncorrect: A model built for a single narrow task is a traditional task-specific model, the opposite of a broadly applicable foundation model. A hand-coded rules engine is not a learned model at all. A cache of answers is a lookup table, not a model that generalizes. A foundation model is the broadly pre-trained, widely adaptable model.

stem: Large language models process text as sequences of which unit, which also drives context limits and per-request pricing?

options.text: Tokens, which are pieces of words

explanationCorrect: LLMs break text into tokens (subword pieces), and the number of tokens determines how much fits in the context window and how much a request costs.
explanationIncorrect: Pixels are the unit of images, not text for a language model. Models do not treat paragraphs as indivisible units; they subdivide text into tokens. Gigabytes measure memory, not the linguistic unit a model consumes. The unit is the token.

stem: You want a model's responses to be more deterministic and focused rather than creative and varied. Which inference parameter do you lower?

options.text: The number of tokens in your prompt

explanationCorrect: Temperature controls randomness in generation: lowering it makes the model favor the most probable next tokens, producing more focused and repeatable output.
explanationIncorrect: Prompt length changes how much context the model has, not how random its sampling is. The parameter count is a fixed property of the model you cannot tune per request. The Region affects where inference runs, not output randomness. The randomness control is temperature.

stem: To find documents semantically similar to a query, you convert text into numeric vectors that place similar meanings close together in vector space. What are these vectors called?
explanationCorrect: Embeddings are dense numeric vectors that capture meaning, so semantically similar text ends up near each other, which is what powers semantic search and retrieval.
explanationIncorrect: Tokens are the subword units of input text, not the meaning vectors used for similarity. Hyperparameters are training configuration values like learning rate. Gradients are values used to update weights during training. The similarity vectors are embeddings.

stem: A model can only consider a limited amount of input text at once when generating a response. What is this limit called?
explanationCorrect: The context window is the maximum amount of text (measured in tokens) a model can take into account at once, bounding how much prompt and history it can use.
explanationIncorrect: The learning rate is a training hyperparameter that controls step size, unrelated to input length at inference. Batch size is how many examples are processed together during training. Epoch count is how many passes over the training data occur. The input-length limit is the context window.

stem: Which AWS service is a generative-AI-powered assistant for business and, in its developer form, for coding and answering AWS questions?
explanationCorrect: Amazon Q is AWS's generative-AI assistant, offered for business use and in a developer variant that helps with coding and AWS-specific questions.
explanationIncorrect: Amazon Athena is a serverless SQL query service over data in S3. Amazon Kinesis handles real-time streaming data. Amazon Neptune is a graph database. The generative-AI assistant is Amazon Q.

stem: You take an existing foundation model and train it further on your own labeled domain data to specialize its behavior. What is this called?

options.text: Pre-training a new model from scratch

explanationCorrect: Fine-tuning continues training a pre-trained model on your own data so it adapts to a specific domain or task without the cost of training from scratch.
explanationIncorrect: Pre-training from scratch builds a model from the ground up on massive data, which is far more expensive and not what adapting an existing model means. Inference is using a finished model to make predictions, not training it. Tokenization is splitting text into tokens. Specializing an existing model on your data is fine-tuning.

stem: You include several examples of the desired input-and-output pattern directly in the prompt so the model follows that pattern. What is this technique called?
explanationCorrect: Providing a handful of worked examples in the prompt is few-shot prompting; the model infers the pattern from those examples at inference time without any weight changes.
explanationIncorrect: Fine-tuning changes the model's weights by training on data; few-shot happens purely in the prompt with no training. Pre-training builds the base model on massive data up front. RLHF is a training-time alignment method using human preference data. Putting examples in the prompt is few-shot prompting.

stem: You ask a model to perform a task using only an instruction, with no examples provided. What is this called?
explanationCorrect: Giving only an instruction and no examples is zero-shot prompting; the model relies entirely on what it learned during pre-training to perform the task.
explanationIncorrect: Few-shot prompting includes example pairs, which this does not. Fine-tuning is additional training on data, not a prompting style. Data augmentation expands a training dataset with transformed samples and is unrelated to how you phrase a single prompt. An instruction with no examples is zero-shot.

stem: You want a managed way to implement RAG on Bedrock: ingest your documents, chunk and embed them, store the vectors, and retrieve relevant context at query time. Which Bedrock feature provides this end to end?
explanationCorrect: Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock is the managed RAG capability: it handles ingestion, chunking, embedding, vector storage, and retrieval, so you get grounded answers without building the pipeline yourself.
explanationIncorrect: Provisioned Throughput reserves dedicated model capacity; it does not build a retrieval pipeline. Amazon Polly is text-to-speech. AWS Batch runs batch compute jobs and is unrelated to retrieval-augmented generation. The managed RAG feature is Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock.

stem: You need a generative AI application to break a request into steps and call external APIs or functions to complete a task, such as looking up an order and then issuing a refund. Which Bedrock capability orchestrates this?
explanationCorrect: Agents for Amazon Bedrock plan a task into steps and invoke the APIs or functions you provide, letting the model take actions rather than only generate text.
explanationIncorrect: Embeddings turn text into vectors for similarity; they do not orchestrate multi-step actions. Temperature tuning adjusts output randomness. Model evaluation compares model quality. The capability that plans steps and calls tools is Agents for Amazon Bedrock.

stem: Your knowledge base changes daily and answers must always reflect the latest documents. Between RAG and fine-tuning, which is generally the better fit, and why?

options.text: RAG, because it retrieves the current documents at query time without retraining the model
Fine-tuning, because you should retrain the model every day on the new documents
Neither; only adjusting temperature keeps answers current
Fine-tuning, because documents baked into the weights stay fresh automatically

explanationCorrect: RAG pulls the latest documents at query time, so new content is reflected immediately with no retraining, which suits a knowledge base that changes daily.
explanationIncorrect: Retraining or fine-tuning every day is slow, costly, and impractical for daily churn. Temperature only affects randomness, not what facts the model can access. Facts baked into weights are frozen at training time and do not update themselves, so fine-tuning is the opposite of fresh. For frequently changing data, RAG is the fit.

stem: You want to compare two foundation models on your task before choosing one, using both automatic metrics and human review. Which Amazon Bedrock capability supports this?
explanationCorrect: Bedrock model evaluation lets you compare models on your data using automatic metrics and human-based evaluation, which is how you choose the right model for a task.
explanationIncorrect: Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity; it does not measure quality. Guardrails filter unsafe content rather than benchmark models. Knowledge Bases implement retrieval, not evaluation. The comparison feature is model evaluation.

stem: Model responses are being cut off too short. Which inference parameter most directly controls the maximum length of the generated output?
explanationCorrect: The maximum output tokens parameter caps how many tokens the model may generate, so raising it lets responses run longer before being truncated.
explanationIncorrect: Temperature changes randomness, not length. Top-p changes which tokens are sampled by cumulative probability, again affecting variety rather than the length cap. Embedding dimension is a property of vector representations, unrelated to generation length. The length cap is the maximum output tokens setting.

stem: For a high-volume, latency-sensitive, and relatively simple classification prompt, which model choice is usually most appropriate?

options.text: A smaller, faster, cheaper model that is sufficient for the task
Always the largest, most expensive model regardless of the task
A text-to-image model repurposed for text classification
No model at all; classify by hand in a spreadsheet

explanationCorrect: Model selection balances cost, latency, and accuracy: for a simple, high-volume task a smaller and faster model that meets the accuracy bar is the economical, responsive choice.
explanationIncorrect: Defaulting to the largest model wastes money and adds latency when a simpler task does not need it. A text-to-image model is the wrong modality for classifying text. Manual classification does not scale to high volume. The appropriate choice is the smallest capable model.

stem: You want an application that accepts an image and answers questions about its contents in text. What kind of foundation model do you need?

options.text: A multimodal model that accepts image input and produces text output

explanationCorrect: Answering questions about an image requires a multimodal model that can take images as input and generate text, combining vision understanding with language output.
explanationIncorrect: A text-only LLM cannot see an image. A text-to-speech model converts text to audio and does not analyze images. An embeddings-only model produces vectors, not conversational text answers. The task needs a multimodal (image-to-text) model.
